result.summary: Clytie, jealous of Leucothoë, tells her father about the Sun's affair, and he buries Leucothoë alive. The Sun cannot revive her and turns her into a frankincense tree, then abandons Clytie, who wastes away and becomes a flower that turns toward him.

scenes.title: Clytie betrays Leucothoë
scenes.summary: Out of envy, Clytie spreads word of the Sun's love for Leucothoë until it reaches Leucothoë's father.
scenes.stakes: Leucothoë risks her father's wrath; Clytie hopes to win back the Sun's love.

scenes.title: Leucothoë buried and transformed
scenes.summary: Her father buries her alive. The Sun clears the sand but cannot revive her, so he sprinkles nectar and she becomes a frankincense tree.
scenes.stakes: Leucothoë's life; the Sun's grief at losing his beloved.

scenes.title: Clytie becomes the sunflower
scenes.summary: The Sun shuns Clytie. She fasts on the bare ground, watching him, and turns into a flower that keeps facing the Sun.
scenes.stakes: Clytie wastes away from unrequited love.

alias_notes.explanation: A patronymic title for the Sun god, also called governor of the winged steeds and author of light.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable closing image of Clytie's constant, unrequited love in flower form.

analysis.text: Jealousy and betrayal bring destruction, and unrequited love becomes endless devotion fixed in a changed shape, typical of Ovid's metamorphoses.
Leucothoë's father punishes her for dishonor, though she says she was forced, reflecting ancient attitudes toward family honor and female blame.

legacy.text: The image of Clytie as the heliotrope or sunflower turning to the sun became a common motif in European poetry and painting.

fun_facts.text: The flower Ovid describes, like a violet, is probably the heliotrope, not the New World sunflower unknown to the Romans.

language_notes.text: 'Son of Hyperion' means the Sun. Hyperion was a Titan, and Ovid often uses this patronymic for the sun god.
'Thou' and 'thee' appear because the narrator suddenly addresses Leucothoë directly in the second person.
Refers to the death of Phaëton, the Sun's son, struck down by Jove's thunderbolt after losing control of the Sun's chariot.
'Odoriferous' means fragrant, sweet-smelling. Nectar is the drink of the gods, here with transforming power.
'Author of light' is a poetic title for the Sun. The parenthesis says love might excuse her grief, and grief excuse her betrayal.

context_notes.text: Clytie was a Nymph who had been loved by the Sun before he turned to Leucothoë, which explains her jealousy.
Frankincense is an aromatic tree resin burned as incense in ancient worship, which gives the transformation a ritual association.

literary_notes.text: The father is shown as 'fierce and unrelenting'; her cry that she was forced makes his cruelty more unjust.
The narrator turns to address the dead Leucothoë directly, adding pathos and intimacy to the scene.
Dew and her own tears serve as her only nourishment, so grief becomes literal sustenance.
The flower turning toward the Sun symbolizes constant, unreturned devotion that outlasts the change of shape.
